extracted.intended_audience: demographers, biostatisticians, and researchers evaluating late-life mortality models
extracted.subtask_description: A formal-comment critique assessing hypotheses and model choices used to infer late-life mortality plateaus, focusing on whether artefacts (age-misreporting, model selection) can explain observed patterns. Emphasizes simulation, sensitivity analyses, empirical error benchmarks, and data-validation scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of alternative hypotheses (age misreporting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Late-life plateaus can be generated by low-frequency, randomly distributed age-misreporting errors; this alternative hypothesis must be explicitly considered and tested rather than assuming biological/evolutionary causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simulate low-frequency age-reporting errors and compare resulting hazard patterns to observed plateaus to determine whether errors alone suffice as an explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity to model choice (age range selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice of age range used to fit log-linear models has a large effect on the size and existence of late-life mortality plateaus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate models fitted to many different age-range combinations (the paper tested 861 combinations between start ages 45–65 and end ages 70–107) and report how the fitted late-life plateau changes; do not rely on a single age-range choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perform explicit simulation of error processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce simulated age-coding errors into synthetic cohorts to test whether such errors produce late-life deceleration or plateaus similar to observed data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use symmetric age-coding errors (e.g., five- and ten-year errors), seed at plausible ages (the paper used age 50), and vary error probabilities across realistic ranges (p = 10^-3 to 10^-6) to show effect on hazard rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify error-rate thresholds that produce artefacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the frequency of age-misreporting errors at which artificial late-life mortality deceleration or plateaus emerge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report thresholds for different model fits (e.g., the Barbi et al. 65–80 model produced plateaus at error frequencies below 1 in 500; a 50–80 model produced artefacts at rates below 1 in 10,000).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use empirical benchmarks for realistic error rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare simulated error rates to observed rates of manual data-entry errors and other empirical sources to judge plausibility of error-based explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference known error rates (e.g., double-entry of clinical trial data: p = 10^-3) and compare cohort-specific contexts (literacy, education) to assess whether required error rates are plausible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess model fit across mid-life and late-life (residual analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine how well a chosen mid-life model predicts late-life data and inspect residuals for skewness or systematic misfit before justifying separate late-life models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot observed hazard rates and model regressions across age; inspect residuals (the paper notes skewed residuals from the 65–80 fit) and consider alternative representative regressions (e.g., 50–80) as comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough sensitivity analysis across many model specifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematically test a wide range of plausible model specifications (e.g., many starting and ending ages for regressions) to determine whether observed phenomena are robust or artefactual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report results from the full grid of tested specifications (the paper’s 861 age-range combinations) and identify whether a single choice produced the largest effect or whether patterns persist broadly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parsimony: prefer simpler error-based explanations when sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: If data-entry or validation errors can recreate observed patterns, these simpler explanations should be preferred over more complex biological or evolutionary interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate that the artefactual model reproduces the observations without invoking cessation of ageing, heterogeneity, or evolutionary mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual plausibility given cohort demographics
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the likelihood of data errors given cohort-specific features such as literacy rates and schooling which affect the probability of age-misreporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical demographic information (e.g., 1904 Italian cohort: 32% literacy, 9.6 months education on average) to argue whether empirically observed error rates are plausible or unlikely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism toward document-based validation alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Documentary validation of ages is not conclusive proof of correctness; previously validated longevity claims have been overturned by clerical errors copied across documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite historical misvalidated cases (e.g., Carrie White) and analyses showing substantial error rates in validated datasets (e.g., 8% error rate in some Gerontology Research Group supercentenarian data) to justify careful scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate similarity between simulated artefacts and observed data
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that hazard rates resulting from simulated errors closely resemble the observed late-life plateau patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide side-by-side comparisons (plots/figures) of observed data points and simulated-model trajectories demonstrating qualitative and quantitative similarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide reproducible code and data for critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the code underlying simulations and analyses available so others can reproduce and evaluate the alternative hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include supporting information (e.g., S1 Code) and explicit descriptions of simulation parameters (error distributions, seeding age, probabilities) to enable replication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report how re-fitting models reduces apparent deviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that re-fitting to alternative age ranges reduces or eliminates the observed late-life plateau, indicating model-dependence of the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare fitted trajectories from alternative regressions and quantify the change in apparent deviation between mid-life and late-life mortality patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete numerical examples to illustrate claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Support qualitative arguments with explicit numerical examples and p-values where relevant (e.g., p = 2 × 10^-4 reported for a simulated deceleration case).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include numeric parameter values, probabilities, and statistical comparisons in figures and text to make the arguments precise and testable.
